The True Effects
of Minimum Wage

When it comes to the minimum wage, everyone has their own beliefs. Some people think it should be higher, lower, or that it shouldn’t exist at all. I’m not here to tell you what to believe, but to show you the facts.

01 / The workers

Who earns the minimum wage?

Of about 145 million wage and salary workers in the United States, 843,000 earn the federal minimum wage or less (0.58%). I expected that the percentage would be closer to 5%. Most are part-time workers (55.9%); however, over a third of them (43.5%) are full-time workers. This is a significantly larger portion than I originally thought; I initially assumed that almost all minimum wage workers would be young people working part-time.

Furthermore, over half of minimum-wage workers (57%) are 25 or older. Again, this was very surprising for the same reason as I said earlier. Out of all of them, 15.5% didn’t finish high school, 34.1% stopped after high school, 23.2% have some college education but no degree, and the remaining have at least an associate's degree. This means that 72.8% of minimum wage workers do not have a college degree.

Data scope · 2024. Reported base hourly pay excludes tips, overtime, and commissions. This group does not include everyone earning a higher state or local minimum. Full time means at least 35 hours; status is unidentified for a small remainder. BLS tables 1 & 6.

02 / Purchasing power

The same wage.
A different cost of living.

In New York, the minimum wage is $16/hour ($17 in NYC). When people argue for an increase in the federal minimum wage, they usually do not think about the nuances in what that means in different places. Below is a chart showing a comparison between how much you would have to make to equal $20 in Rochester, a city in NY. Take Manhattan, for example; you would have to make about $46 there to have the same spending power as $20 in Rochester, NY. This shows the difficulty in establishing a federal minimum wage. You cannot base it on Manhattan and pay everyone $45/hour, so how do you find a middle ground?

New York rates: Effective January 1, 2026, $17 also applies to Long Island and Westchester; $16 applies to the rest of the state. NY Department of Labor. The chart below compares living costs, not legal wage floors.

03 / The evidence

Hourly pay is only part
of the equation.

Bils, Kaymak & Wu · Brazil

One paper written by Mark Bils, Bariş Kaymak, and Kai-Jie Wu concluded that while a raise in the minimum wage can help workers by making it difficult for employers to impose wage markdowns, it can also exceed the productivity of some workers. If the minimum wage increases to the point where an employer's least productive workers are not profitable, they could lose their jobs. In this scenario, as the minimum wage increases, the lowest-paid workers' wages actually decrease; the workers would lose their formal employment, potentially shifting into lower-paying informal jobs. Now, this study used data collected from Brazil, so this should not be seen as a conclusive “this is going to happen in America”; however, it is something to be aware of as a possibility.

Evidence type: The minimum-wage result is a prediction from a model calibrated to Brazil, not a measured U.S. policy effect. Leaving formal employment need not mean leaving all employment. Read the assigned paper.
Neumark & Wohl · United States

Another paper by Neumark and Wohl, “Do Minimum Wages Help Workers in Poor and Low-Income Families?” uses U.S. survey data from 2003–2016 to measure the effects of minimum wage on workers based on income levels. For the low-wage workers, their data show a similar effect as the first paper: higher minimum wages reduce the probability of initially employed low-wage workers remaining employed. Despite finding adverse effects for initially low-waged workers, there is not a consistent pattern of increasingly negative effects for the poorest workers. Even if wages are higher on paper, a higher hourly rate does not necessarily mean higher total income. For example, consider someone working for $10/hour for 30 hours per week, vs. $12 for 24 hours per week; the first makes $300 while the second makes $288. This shows one way employers could offset an increase in minimum wage by reducing hours of employment. [Paper]

04 / The bigger picture

Wages, work, and poverty.

Now, this is a lot of information, but what does it actually mean? The bottom line is that when it comes to targeting poverty, there are severe limitations to using minimum wage policy. The 10th percentile of wage workers in America is $15/hour; this is over double the federal minimum wage. The 25th percentile is $18.07, and the median is $24.51.

Further, in 2024, about 0.58% of wage and salary workers make at or below the federal minimum wage of $7.25/hour. In 2024, there were 35.9 million Americans in poverty. Even if every single minimum wage earner was a part of that number, they would still only make up 2.35%. When it comes to raising the federal minimum wage, the argument is more nuanced than that an increase in wages will help people in poverty.

There are both potential benefits for those who will end up being paid more as well as costs for workers whose hours or employment decrease.

The percentile headcounts follow the assignment’s approximation that OEWS percentiles also describe hourly workers. They combine 2024 hourly-worker counts with the intended May 2025 wage distribution, which includes salaried pay expressed hourly. These are approximate headcounts, not direct OEWS counts. The workforce estimate is an annual average and excludes self-employment; it is not total employment at year-end.
